slides.title: No secrets in the bundle
slides.summary: Anything shipped to the browser is public: API keys, internal URLs, feature flags and comments.
body: Build tools inline environment variables into JavaScript. If a variable is in the bundle, it's public.

ul: Publishable keys only: keys meant to be public (Stripe publishable key, a map key restricted by referrer) are fine.
Secret keys stay on a server: proxy calls through your backend, which adds the key.
Source maps expose your original code. Upload them to your error tracker instead of serving them publicly, if that matters to you.
Hidden UI isn't access control: hiding an admin button doesn't stop someone calling the admin API.

body: <mark>If the browser can read a value, so can the user and any script on the page.</mark>

cells.text: Yes, but assume users can flip them
Mirror them for UX; enforce on the server

slides.title: Where to keep auth tokens
slides.summary: localStorage is readable by any XSS. HttpOnly cookies aren't, but need CSRF protection.
body: Every storage option is a trade-off between XSS and CSRF exposure.

ul: localStorage / sessionStorage: easy, but any script on the page can read the token and send it anywhere.
In memory: gone on reload; still usable by XSS while the page is open, but not easily stolen for later.
HttpOnly cookie: JavaScript can't read it at all. The browser sends it automatically, so you must defend against CSRF.

body: <mark>Prefer HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies for session tokens, and keep tokens short-lived.</mark>

body.text: A small server on your own origin does the OAuth flow, keeps the access and refresh tokens server-side, and gives the browser only an HttpOnly session cookie. Current OAuth guidance for browser apps recommends this as the most secure option.

slides.title: OAuth in single-page apps
slides.summary: Use the Authorization Code flow with PKCE. The implicit flow is deprecated.
body: A browser app can't keep a client secret, so it uses PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) to prove the app that started the login is the one finishing it.

ul: Never use the old implicit flow, which put tokens in the URL.
Keep access tokens short-lived (minutes) and use refresh token rotation.
Validate the state parameter to stop login CSRF.

steps.caption: The app makes a one-time secret and sends only its hash.
The user signs in on the identity provider.
A short-lived code comes back, not a token.
Only the app holding the verifier can turn the code into tokens.
